topics.title: Decision Trees
topics.summary: A decision tree predicts by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the data, following one branch per answer until it reaches a final answer.

image.alt: Animation frame titled Random Forest: many random trees voting, with a Python snippet that grows trees on 500 customers.
image.caption: A random forest grows many decision trees and takes a majority vote (example from your screenshots).

terms.definition: The first question, at the top of the tree. Every prediction starts here.
A question about one feature, such as 'Exam score ≥ 50?'.
One possible answer to a question (Yes/No), leading to the next node.
An end point that holds the prediction, for example Pass or Fail.
A measurable input (exam score) and the cut-off value the question compares against (50).
Scores a training algorithm uses to pick the question that separates the classes best.
A tree so deep it memorises the training data and does badly on new data.
Many trees trained on random samples of the data; the final answer is their majority vote.

example.title: Predict pass or fail
example.body: A teacher writes down a rule set: if the exam score is at least 50 and attendance is at least 75%, predict Pass; otherwise predict Fail. The tree below encodes exactly that.
example.note: This tree is written by hand to teach the idea. It was NOT trained on data. A trained tree chooses its own questions and thresholds from examples.

io.input: A record of features, for example exam score 62 and attendance 60%.
steps: Compare the feature with the node's threshold.
Follow the Yes or No branch.
Repeat until you reach a leaf.
io.output: The leaf's label, here Fail (score passes, but attendance 60% is below 75%).

exercise.prompt: A student scored 48 and attended 90% of classes. Using the tree, what is the prediction, and which nodes did you visit?
exercise.hint: Start at the root and answer one question at a time.
exercise.solution: Fail. Root: score 48 ≥ 50? No, so you go straight to the Fail leaf. Attendance is never checked.

quiz.q: What does a leaf node contain?
quiz.why: Leaves are end points that hold the predicted outcome.

quiz.q: In the example tree, a student scores 62 with 60% attendance. What is predicted?
quiz.why: 62 ≥ 50 is Yes, but attendance 60% < 75% is No, which leads to Fail.

quiz.q: Why can a very deep tree perform badly on new data?
quiz.why: Deep trees memorise noise in the training set (overfitting).

quiz.q: How does a random forest make its final decision?
quiz.why: Each tree votes and the most common answer wins.

topics.title: Word Analysis (NLP)
topics.summary: Natural language processing turns text into numbers a model can work with, so it can find keywords, judge sentiment, sort topics and summarise.

image.alt: Each word of 'Never gonna give you up' shown as an arrow (vector) on a 2D grid, with x_i in R^d above.
image.caption: Each word becomes a vector x_i ∈ ℝ^d. Real models use hundreds of dimensions; the picture shows two.

terms.definition: A small piece of text, usually a word or part of a word.
Splitting text into tokens.
Very common words (the, is, of) often ignored when finding keywords.
A list of numbers that represents a word's meaning, so similar words sit close together.
A score for how important a word is in one text compared with many texts.
Predicting whether text is positive, negative or neutral.
A real-world thing mentioned in text, such as a person, place or company.
A mechanism letting a model weigh which other words matter most when reading each word.

example.title: Is this review positive?
example.body: The sentence 'The lesson was clear and helpful' is split into tokens, each token becomes a vector, and a classifier outputs a prediction such as positive with a probability.
example.note: Sentiment is a prediction with uncertainty, not a fact. Sarcasm and context can fool it.

io.input: Raw text, for example a sentence or review.
steps: Convert each token to a vector (embedding).
The model combines the vectors and scores each possible label.
io.output: A label (positive/negative), keywords or a summary, ideally with a confidence value.

exercise.prompt: Tokenize 'Never gonna give you up' and say how many tokens you get. Would 'the' and 'of' be useful keywords in a longer text?
exercise.hint: Split on spaces; think about how common stop words are.
exercise.solution: Five tokens: Never, gonna, give, you, up. Stop words like 'the' and 'of' appear everywhere, so they rarely work as keywords.

quiz.why: Tokenization breaks text into words or sub-words.

options: A word as a list of numbers capturing meaning
quiz.why: Embeddings place words as vectors; similar meanings end up close.

quiz.q: A sentiment model says 'positive, 0.62'. How should you treat that?
quiz.why: Classifier outputs are probabilities, not guarantees.

quiz.q: Which is usually a poor keyword?
quiz.why: Stop words like 'the' occur in almost every text.

topics.title: Picture Analysis (Computer Vision)
topics.summary: Computer vision turns an image into numbers (pixels), finds patterns in them, and outputs labels, objects or descriptions.

image.alt: A 4x4 pixel patch with 3 colour channels flattened into 48 numbers, multiplied by a learned matrix W to give a vector.
image.caption: Patch embedding: a 4×4×3 patch = 48 numbers, turned into a vector by a learned matrix W.

terms.definition: The smallest dot of an image, stored as numbers.
The red, green and blue values (0–255) that make up a colour pixel.
A small square block of pixels cut from the image.
Flattening a patch into numbers and multiplying by a learned matrix to get a vector.
Giving the whole image one label, such as 'cat'.
Finding objects and drawing a bounding box around each.
How strongly the model favours its answer. It is not a guarantee of being right.
A sliding filter that highlights edges and textures in an image.

example.title: One patch becomes a vector
example.body: A 4×4 patch with 3 colour channels has 48 numbers (R 220, G 234, B 247, …). Multiplying them by a learned matrix W gives a shorter vector. A vision transformer does this for every patch, then lets attention compare patches.
example.note: The numbers in the picture are an illustration from your screenshot, not output from this app's models.

io.input: An image file (pixels with colour channels).
steps: Flatten each patch and embed it as a vector.
Layers (attention or convolution) combine the patches.
io.output: A label, or boxes with labels, and a confidence score when the model provides one.

exercise.prompt: How many numbers describe an 8×8 RGB patch before embedding?

quiz.q: How many numbers describe a 4×4 RGB patch?
Classification differs from detection because classification…
quiz.why: Detection finds and boxes each object; classification gives one label.

options: The model strongly favours that answer
quiz.why: Confidence is the model's own score, and models can be confidently wrong.

quiz.q: What does the matrix W in patch embedding do?
options: Maps patch numbers to a vector, and is learned
quiz.why: W is learned during training and converts raw patch values into useful features.

topics.title: Model Training and Evaluation
topics.summary: Training fits a model to examples; evaluation checks it on data it has never seen, so you know whether it really learned or just memorised.

image.alt: Random forest animation with code that trains 100 trees on the first 400 of 500 customers and tests on the last 100.
image.caption: From the screenshot's code: 500 customers, trees grown on 400, accuracy checked on the held-out last 100.

terms.definition: Examples with measurable inputs (features) and the answer to learn (label).
Train fits the model, validation tunes it, test gives a final honest score on unseen data.
A setting chosen before training, such as tree depth or number of trees.
Memorising the training set versus being too simple to learn the pattern.
Share of predictions that are correct.
Precision: of the predicted positives, how many are right. Recall: of the real positives, how many were found.
A table of correct and wrong predictions per class.
Test information sneaking into training, which inflates scores.
Prompting only gives instructions to a finished model. Fine-tuning updates its weights with new data. Training from scratch builds a model from random weights.

example.title: 500 customers, 100 trees
example.body: Split 500 customer records: 400 for training, 100 held out for testing. Grow 100 random trees on the 400, let them vote, and measure accuracy only on the held-out 100. That honest score estimates how it behaves on new customers.
example.note: Sending prompts to a hosted language model is inference. It is not training or fine-tuning.

steps: Split into train, validation and test.
Pick an algorithm and train it.
Score once on the test set, then save and monitor.
io.output: A saved model, its metrics and metadata, used for predictions.

exercise.prompt: A model catches 30 of 50 real fraud cases and wrongly flags 10 normal cases (so 40 flags in total). Compute precision and recall.
exercise.hint: Precision = correct flags ÷ all flags. Recall = correct flags ÷ real cases.

quiz.q: Why keep a separate test set?
options: To measure performance on unseen data
quiz.why: Scoring on training data hides overfitting.

quiz.q: Training accuracy 99%, test accuracy 70%. Most likely problem?
quiz.why: A big train/test gap signals memorisation.

quiz.q: Does sending prompts to a language model train it?
quiz.why: Prompting changes the input, not the model's weights.

qa.answer: A decision tree predicts by asking a chain of yes/no questions about the input. Each question is a node, each answer is a branch, and a leaf holds the predicted outcome, such as Pass or Fail.
questions: how does a decision tree work
can you tell me what decision trees are

qa.answer: The root node is the first question at the top. Decision nodes ask further questions, branches are the Yes/No answers, and leaf nodes at the ends hold the final prediction.
questions: what are leaf nodes in a decision tree
difference between root node and leaf node
what are the parts of a decision tree

qa.answer: When training, the algorithm tries possible questions and keeps the one that separates the classes best, measured with Gini impurity or information gain. It repeats this on each branch until it reaches a stopping rule.
questions: how does a decision tree choose which question to ask
how are splits chosen in a tree
explain gini and entropy for splitting

qa.answer: A random forest trains many decision trees on random samples of the data and takes a majority vote of their predictions. Voting cancels out each tree's individual mistakes, so it overfits less than one deep tree.
questions: how does a random forest work
why use many trees instead of one
explain majority voting in random forests

qa.answer: Natural language processing (NLP) is how computers work with text. It converts words into numbers, then uses models to find keywords, judge sentiment, sort topics or summarise.
Tokenization splits text into small pieces called tokens, usually words or parts of words. Models read tokens, not raw letters.
questions: how is text split into tokens

qa.answer: An embedding turns a word into a list of numbers (a vector) so that words with similar meanings sit close together. This lets a model compare and combine words mathematically.
questions: how do computers turn words into numbers
why are words represented as vectors

qa.answer: Sentiment analysis predicts whether text is positive, negative or neutral. It is a prediction with uncertainty, because sarcasm and context can mislead it.
questions: how can a computer tell if text is positive or negative

qa.answer: Computer vision lets computers analyse images. An image is stored as numbers, a model finds patterns in them, and it outputs labels, detected objects or descriptions.
questions: what is image analysis in ai

qa.answer: A pixel is the smallest dot of an image. In colour images each pixel has three numbers, the red, green and blue channels, usually from 0 to 255.
questions: how is an image stored as numbers
how does a computer represent a picture

qa.answer: Vision transformers cut an image into small square patches, flatten each patch into numbers (a 4x4 RGB patch gives 48), and multiply by a learned matrix to get a vector. Attention then compares the patches.
questions: how do vision transformers split an image
how does attention work on images

qa.answer: Image classification gives the whole image one label. Object detection finds each object and draws a bounding box around it. A confidence score is the model's own certainty, and it can still be wrong.
questions: difference between image classification and object detection
what does a confidence score mean

qa.answer: Data is split into a training set (fit the model), a validation set (tune settings) and a test set (one final honest score on unseen data). Keeping them separate reveals overfitting.
questions: what is a train test split
why split data into training validation and test sets
what is a test set for
explain training validation and test data

qa.answer: Overfitting is when a model memorises its training data and does badly on new data. Underfitting is when it is too simple to learn the pattern. Fixes include more data, simpler models, limiting tree depth and validating on held-out data.
questions: why does my model do well on training data but badly on new data

qa.answer: Accuracy is the share of correct predictions. Precision is how many predicted positives were right, recall is how many real positives were found, and F1 combines the two. A confusion matrix shows all the counts.
questions: what is accuracy precision and recall
what is the difference between precision and recall
how do you evaluate a classification model

qa.answer: Prompting only gives instructions to a finished model; that is inference, not training. Fine-tuning updates a model's weights with new examples. Training from scratch builds a model from random weights.
questions: what is the difference between prompting and fine-tuning
does prompting an ai train it
what does training from scratch mean
is sending prompts to a model the same as training it

qa.answer: I keep a small set of learned knowledge about AI basics. For each question I compute a similarity-based confidence score; when it is above a threshold calibrated on held-out examples I answer from what I learned, and otherwise your message goes to the app's other models.
questions: when are you sure of an answer
when do you use what you have learned
how do you decide to answer by yourself
what happens when you are not sure
do you fall back to other models when unsure
